- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce forecast peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and forecast is rising, cap upward movement at 1–2% above recent high to prevent overcorrection.
- When sentiment swings from positive to negative, model tends to overreact — dampen forecast slope by 15–20% in the first 5 days.
- If recent history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of downward trend), forecast should not exceed 1.5x recent high unless sentiment confirms strong bullish momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.7), model often overestimates volatility — reduce forecast variance by 10–15%.
- If forecast spikes after a strong sentiment rally, reduce the spike’s magnitude by 10–15% to account for market correction.
- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.1) over 5+ days, forecast should be capped at 1–2% below recent low to avoid false bullishness.
- If forecast is consistently above true outcome by 2–3% over 3–5 days, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to align with mean reversion.
- For sentiment history with alternating highs/lows, model tends to overfit — apply smoothing filter to forecast (e.g., 3-day moving average) to reduce noise.
